utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning to the technical booth, the interpreters; good morning to the legal assistants and the registrar. Since we are seeing one another after a long break and we see some new faces on both sides, perhaps we could begin with the appearances. Office of the Prosecutor, please. Mrs. Somers, could you please introduce your team.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Susan Linda Somers for the Prosecution. Also Mr. Kapila Waidyaratne, Ms. Denise Gustin, and Mr. Daniel Saxon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. The Defence in the normal order, please. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. The Defence of Mr. Kvocka consists of Krstan Simic and Branko Lukic, as usual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much. Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. The Defence for the accused Kos consists of Mrs. Nikolic, Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan, and myself, Zarko Nikolic, again, as usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Toma Fila. Together with Mr. Zoran Jovanovic, we represent the accused Mr. Radic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good morning. Our Defence team has been somewhat enlarged. We have with us Mrs. Ljiljana Mitrovic from Belgrade, our legal assistant; Mr. Miodrag Deretic, an attorney from Prijedor; and I am Slobodan Stojanovic, attorney from Belgrade. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. The Defence of Mr. Prcac consists of myself, Mr. Jovan Simic, and my colleague from Belgrade, Mr. Masic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I should like to take advantage of the opportunity to wish everyone in the courtroom and those assisting us -- there seems to be a problem with the headphones. Is it working now? No? Yes? Yes? Can everyone hear me now? Maybe the problem is due to the wrong selection of the channel. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We happen to have the same problem as our client. We are not getting the interpretation, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the solution will be the same in your case too. Is it working now? Can you hear me now? I see you nodding so you do hear me, Mr. Stojanovic. Very well. Anyway, I was saying that I should like to take advantage of this opportunity to greet everyone and to wish everyone a Happy New Year. We are going to now engage in the preparations for today's hearing. As you know, we are holding this Status Conference in order to discuss the pre-trial briefs of the Defence and to prepare for the Defence case. I, therefore, suggest the following agenda: For the Pre-Defence Conference, we will be working on the cross-examination of the accused Kvocka and Radic and the testimony of other accused who wish to testify. I will later explain the reasons. The Chamber would like to address this question separately. After that, we are going to deal with the Defence witnesses and the exhibits that we need to review. We also have several outstanding motions, some of which need to be discussed in private session. So we will begin with those points and later on we will address the motions I have mentioned. The agenda item has to do with the cross-examination of Kvocka and Radic and the examination-in-chief of other accused who wish to testify. Unforeseen circumstances have created room for the Chamber to meet, which means we plan to work next week but the Chamber, which is always concerned with efficiency and the desire to maintain good relations with the parties, would like to suggest to the parties that we do work next week. As you know, we do not have the problem of the presence of witnesses because, if we begin with the cross-examination of Mr. Kvocka and Mr. Radic and the testimony of other accused, then we don't have the problem of witnesses' presence or not. If the first place, therefore, I should like to consult the parties to see whether, yes or no, we could begin -- instead of beginning on the 22nd, whether we could begin on the 15th. It is true that we will have plenty of time afterwards to discuss all these matters - the list of witnesses, the list of exhibits, and so on - but I should like to hear the initial reaction of the parties, that is, the Defence counsel, and see to what extent this suggestion could be acceptable. We're fully aware that we are changing a little bit the work plan, and that's why we're discussing it. If yes, fine; if not, again fine. But in this way we could speed things up a little and gain some time. So I should like to begin with Mr. Krstan Simic to see whether you are in a position to respond. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I must say that we are caught by surprise. We had a programme and a plan of our own. On Tuesday I have to deal with some very important problems linked to witnesses, so I'm afraid that we might gain time at this stage and we would be wasting time later on because we have a lot of problems with visas and other requirements linked to witnesses. I think this is a problem. But should the others agree, I'll find a way around it, but for us, in principle, it is not acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the Chamber feels that we need two weeks for the cross-examination of the accused and the testimony of the other accused, at least, so we would have plenty of time to deal with the other matters later on. But let me hear the other Defence counsel first. Mr. Nikolic -- I see Mr. O'Sullivan on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning. On behalf of Kos, we won't make any comments regarding Radic or Kvocka's cross-examination. As far as Mr. Kos is concerned, if he should testify, we submit it should be during his Defence case. And the second point connected to that is that we have not yet determined whether or not he will testify, but if he does, it should be during his Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. O'Sullivan. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, apart from being surprised, that is not important, but there is another prior problem we have to deal with. Talking to Ms. Somers, it is the Prosecution opinion that the cross-examination of Kvocka, Radic, Prcac, Zigic, or any other one of the others that might want to testify should be done at the end of the whole case. In this way, we would begin with the cross-examination of Kvocka and Radic. We don't know whether the other three would testify, and there would be a lack of continuity. You know that I'm always in a hurry and I'm eager to speed things up, but I don't think that we'll be able to do so in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Anyway, the Chamber too has been taken by surprise, but we're trying to make the best of our time. But still, I would like to hear all the Defence counsel. Mr. Stojanovic, what are your impressions? What is your reaction?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that our Defence team is not prepared for such a change because it would upset seriously the preparations for our case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jovan Simic. Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at this point Mr. Prcac's Defence is least affected. We could accept your suggestion, though it would upset our own programme of meetings with some witnesses, so I don't think it is realistic or opportune to make this change. But, of course, we will abide by your ruling, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Jovan Simic. Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, under normal circumstances, I would be elated at having the extra time in court. Under these circumstances, however, earlier last week I contacted Mr. Fourmy in order to let the Chamber know that Mr. Saxon and I would not be in The Hague until Tuesday evening, the 16th. And in the event that this particular hearing were to carry over, which is what we thought might happen, we would have respectfully requested the Chamber to have scheduled it so as not to conflict with its own schedule, of course, with Krstic, and then just to know our availability. So in fact we have made arrangements based on having made that representation to Mr. Fourmy and subsequently confirming that we had made plans, accordingly, not to be here. That is the first point. So in fact, that is the case. The second issue is about the order of cross-examination of the two accused who have previously given their direct exam in an unusual order but certainly by agreement. And we had, as Ms. Hollis had mentioned at the last Status Conference, expressed, after Your Honours' inquiry, a preference based on the planning for these accused to be cross-examined at the end of their case. I think that the history of the, as it were, concession or the change in normal order left it -- it appeared to have left it, from what I read in the transcript, as what the Prosecutor wants to do, and we have taken advantage of that language. It would be a change for us. We've planned around that, and assuming that the Court had accepted Ms. Hollis's statement of preference. So indeed it would be difficult on two levels. And if the Court would care at this time for argument on our position about the order of the cross-examination of the two accused, I would be happy to do so, or I shall wait until it's on the agenda. I do apologise for any inconvenience that we might have worked. As I say, normally we would be delighted to have the extra time in court. Just because of the timing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So I think we have to go on to an analysis of other matters. And to be realistic, it doesn't seem to be convenient for the majority to make any change in the timetable. But anyway, we have a lot of work to do next week. So I think we should now go on to the other issues, and that is the list of witnesses, or perhaps the Pre-Trial briefs, the list of Defence witnesses, and the list of exhibits. Perhaps we could take the two together to be covered by several speakers. I don't know whether the Defence has had the opportunity to review the response of the Prosecutor, and there is a whole series of questions, some which might be responded to briefly and quickly; others I don't know whether the parties could agree on in a way that the Chamber could accept; and then there are other matters on which decisions will have to be taken. There are certain aspects on which the Chamber should reserve its opinion because the parties cannot reach an agreement or because it is up to the Chamber to decide. So let us embark upon this matter to see where we stand with respect to the list of witnesses, the list of exhibits, and perhaps envisage for next week another Status Conference to review things. But in any event, we'll see how the discussion will develop. Perhaps I should give the floor to each Defence counsel on condition that they are all familiar with the response of the Prosecutor. Then they could react. And after that, perhaps I could give the floor to Ms. Susan Somers to respond to all the responses of the Defence counsel. Would you agree with that procedure? Yes? Fine. Or the other possibility is to give the floor to Ms. Susan Somers, who is going to say, "I need this and that," "My position is such-and-such," and then we could see whether Defence counsel can respond. Perhaps that would be better. Perhaps, Ms. Susan Somers, you should take the floor first to tell us what your reaction is to the briefs of the Defence and what your requests are with respect to the Defence counsel. Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is my hope that counsel have had an opportunity to have reviewed our response. We tried to provide, I believe by immediate delivery yesterday, in advance of the deadline, the document, so as to be ready for this morning. Some of the issues, Your Honours, concern several specific witnesses for whom pseudonyms have been affixed; others concern generally the extensive use of affidavit; and others concern the discussion about deposition. I would like to inform the Chamber - I believe we did set this forward in our response - that our Office invited the Defence to meet with us and discuss in advance these issues. We thought it would probably save some time in framing or reducing the time and to clarify issues. One particular matter -- actually, no. One general matter is something I wanted to immediately bring to the Court's attention because it will affect, perhaps, timing and that is the notion of deposition as opposed to videolink. The history of the deposition in this case appears to have arisen before this Chamber was seized of the matter because the case essentially sat hovering, waiting for a trial date. It was, I think, a very wise suggestion on the part of both Judge May and Mr. Niemann and counsel to find some, at that time, solution under rather exceptional circumstances. We are clearly well on the way, and I think those circumstances have changed whereby the use of videolink, which affords the Chamber the advantage or the benefit of live testimony and questioning, which, as my viewing of this Chamber has been, is an active part of the practice, as well as the opportunity, certainly, to get a general sense of all other aspects of reliability and credibility. It is certainly the position of the Prosecution that unless there is a real life/death, literally, type issue at this point, or one of such grave health concerns, that if there is to be a remote means of taking testimony, it should be by videolink. It involves a reasonable amount of preparation in advance, and therefore we would have to, amongst ourselves and with the Chamber's guidance, set the order so that we wouldn't have to go back and forth. We have indicated to counsel that we certainly have no objection to holding these matters in Banja Luka, which I believe would be the forum of convenience for many of the witnesses. I wanted immediately to throw that out to the Chamber because if, in fact, that has to be factored in for timing rather than, again, a back and forth, we can try to work it out that we have our parties there and that the technical aspects are set up. Even if depositions were undertaken, there is a technical side to them as well, but this, in our view, is the best all-around way for the Chamber to see and participate in, as it has always done, this type of examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Can I ask you a question?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You talked about your vast preference being for videolink as opposed to deposition. I'm wondering - I read your paper last night - if that is a general policy of the Prosecution. Let me be specific. In another case in which this Chamber is involved, the Prosecution has itself put forth and actually been given permission for 23 depositions. This was the Prosecution's policy in order to expedite the trial. They did limit it, and we limited it in our order, to what were called subsidiary witnesses; in other words, not witnesses dealing with the most vital actions or behaviour, but background, jurisdictional, other issues. And I find it difficult to reconcile that with a position which says that depositions should not be used except where health does permit it. Also, I wish to bring to your attention - you probably know already - that the Prosecution submitted proposals to the Plenary Session of the -- or to the Rules Committee which would greatly make more flexible the use of many of the things which you oppose in here. I'm wondering, do we have a Prosecution policy or do we have a different policy for each Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Judge Wald, this is more specific to this case. This is not -- this is because the reason for wanting to get so many depositions going -- in principle, as provided for in the Rules, it is a very viable tool when used prudently. There are certain types of witnesses who, I think, in our judgement, should not not be before the Bench. The concern in the Kvocka case was that we would not get started, and this was to get us started. Also, I believe it was discussed at a time before the witness lists were refined and pared down to a more sure number. A number of these -- a number of the witnesses for whom depositions has been suggested or would be suggested are witnesses who would address key, very disputed issues, core issues to this indictment or to the charges. So, no, of course, as a tool provided for in the Rules, I'm aware that it will be invoked. But in this particular case, I think the circumstances under which it originally was raised have changed, unless there is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Just to follow through. I understand and can understand an argument made that a particular witness should not be deposed because it's a critical witness and you want to have the opportunity via videolink or live testimony. But there were suggestions, or at least I read them as such, in your written motion, and I think they were echoed in your oral motion, that as a general notion, we don't think depositions ought to be used unless there's illness or there's some vital reason. I did find that to be quite at odds with other advocacy of the Prosecution in other cases, as well as in its general Rules, and I wanted to clarify that. I understand if you say, "Not this witness because this witness has got key material," but not, "No depositions because we don't think they are a good idea unless somebody is physically ill."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Entirely my fault, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: We just wanted to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm not representing a policy of the entire office. I'm looking at the history of this particular case and why it arose in this case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So you would agree that we should -- we, the Chamber, in deciding whether a deposition was appropriate, should look at the particular witness and what that particular witness proposes to testify to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Very much so, Your Honour. I think that is critical.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers, with your permission, I should like to introduce a new perspective in this debate. It is true you mentioned the specific character of this particular case, and I do understand your position. You make mention in your response of the principle of equality of arms which has been invoked in this case on a number of occasions. You know that we managed to reach a compromise because the depositions were quite opposite and extreme at the beginning. It is perfectly natural for a case involving five accused, that each of him has his idea of how to approach a particular problem. So we considered this problem of depositions from that particular perspective. But there is something new that I should like to introduce in the present debate. Let us try not to think of the depositions. We have so far focused on the principle of orality of testimony and on the presence of witnesses in the courtroom, and such principle never took place for the Prosecution. We should like to try to see who are the witnesses whose presence in the courtroom is necessary and important. All other witnesses could be heard by way of affidavits and depositions. I think it would be more practical and more efficient to proceed in that way because if we continue to think about depositions only, I think it is going to cause us a lot of problems and involve additional costs. So I should like to appeal to the parties to take this particular aspect into account: to have a look at the list of witnesses once again and try to decide who are the witnesses who should be brought physically to the courtroom; as regards other witnesses, to see if it would be possible to hear them via affidavits and depositions. I think that we have so far good case law in that respect, and I think it would be very useful for the parties to make use of this provision. Let me give you a couple of guidelines as regards the use of lists of witnesses in this way. Now, we should perhaps see who are the important witnesses and who are the witnesses who have to be brought into the courtroom. We also have to bear in mind the use of time when it comes to the physical appearance of the witness in the courtroom. I'm not going to be more specific than this. I hope that you know what I have in mind. To bring a witness here to the courtroom and to hear him, to examine him, for only half an hour, maybe that is not a very important witness in that case. Maybe such a witness could be heard via affidavit or deposition. I do not wish to offend anyone's position here, but I'm afraid that we are running the risk of transforming this Tribunal into a travel agency, because we are simply forcing witnesses to spend a long time travelling, we spend a lot of money doing that, and eventually the witness spends only 30 minutes in the courtroom. I know that things cannot be approached from that angle only. But we have to bear in mind the fact that there is the quantitative aspect and the qualitative aspect of the problem. If it is absolutely necessary to bring a witness here and to examine him for about 30 minutes maybe, then that's fine, but one should perhaps ask oneself beforehand whether it is really necessary to bring such a witness to testify before the Chamber. So the list of witnesses should be reviewed once again from that perspective, and we should see whether it's really necessary for such witnesses to be brought here. On the basis of that, we will reach appropriate conclusions and review the list of witnesses. Of course, we have to bear in mind the equality of arms here and the criterion that was applied to the Prosecution was the following: You have a certain amount of time and it is up to you to make use of that time. However, there are certain aspects of the problem which have to be taken into consideration here, because it is different when we have to bring five witnesses for two weeks or 50 witnesses for the same period of time. So this also involves the economical aspect of the procedure. I do not want to impose certain restrictions in terms of time to you because it's finally up to you to decide. Each one of the accused has his idea of his defence and his case, and it's eventually up to you to decide. I have, perhaps, mentioned too many things at once, too many new elements for this debate, and I apologise for doing that. But please bear in mind the position of the Chamber, that is, that we should perhaps leave aside, forget about the depositions at this point in time and think about other possible approaches to the issue. Sorry once again for having interrupted you, Ms. Somers. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No problem at all, Your Honour. Thank you for clarifying the Chamber's position on this and giving us some guidance. I do want to indicate to the Chamber that, in discussions with my learned opponents, the concerns of many of the witnesses who are not coming to The Hague are because of penal interest, and therefore live here would not have been an option for them one way or the other. So in trying to accommodate the concerns, and realising we will certainly, where a number of these witnesses will be critical for us, want the opportunity to cross-examine, these would be the most important witnesses to bring to the Chamber's attention. On issues -- I beg your pardon, I'm losing my voice. But also where, in the affidavit arena, the witness -- we may raise an objection, and if the Chamber admits the affidavit over objection, at least several of counsel were generous enough to indicate that they would present their witness for cross-examination if the Chamber permitted us to do so. And again, if these are the same witnesses who are concerned about making a personal appearance in The Hague, we would have to do this again in videolink. And all I would ask the Chamber to help us craft is some means of organising those witnesses who would be properly the subject of video live testimony, for whatever reasons - in the Defence's eyes, their legitimate penal interests - then we would be very grateful for that assistance. And where it appears to be appropriate to use the other means provided for in the Rules, we will abide by the Chamber's decision. Excuse me one minute.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Unless the Chamber wishes for us to go accused by accused, if it is acceptable to -- we stand on our positions that we have tried to articulate in advance for you to look at. And if there are questions perhaps that may arise on our position - excuse me - during the positions asserted by the Defence, may we then have an opportunity to respond at that time to know if there's a change from anything that's been given to us in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, I'm sorry. I apologise. Judge Wald? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I just had one question on your affidavit position. You seem to have, with reference to several possible witnesses, opposed using the 94 ter affidavit route because you said that they appeared to be testifying about essential facts in dispute and you thought that violated the spirit of 94 ter. If not, as you are well aware, the actual Rule doesn't draw a distinction between so-called essential and -- or essential or critical; it just says "a fact in dispute." And I just wanted to clarify that. Your position is that affidavits, even if they meet technically the requirements laid down by the Court of Appeal in that they are direct, they have a direct nexus with the testimony of some live witnesses and the technical advance notice requirements, that they're still inappropriate for witnesses who are testifying about core issues? Is that your position, or what? I just wanted to make sure I had it right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Judge Wald, partly yes, partly no. Certainly on issues that are absolutely focal, and particularly where someone whose role or whose knowledge may be crucial for our proof, we would need, and I think under the general -- under 20, 21, we would be entitled to try to -- or we would be obligated to get the truth before the Bench by carrying out a very effective cross-examination. Your Honour is absolutely correct. Disputed fact is the definition, but the appellate decision gives a fair amount of discretion to the Chamber in the use of them, and we would ask this Chamber if it would like us to specify exactly which individuals following -- or if at the next conference we should discuss this. We would be very happy to do that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers, the next -- as regards the next Status Conference, we will see about that. But I have a question for you. You have had contact with Defence counsel. Are you under the impression that you are likely to reach an agreement sometime soon or is it your opinion that no agreement is possible? As far as I understand, Defence counsel intimated that it would be possible to cross-examine witnesses even if they testify through affidavits. So do you think that there is a possibility for that or not, that is, a possibility of reaching an agreement with the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, my perception of our meetings was one of guarded optimism in terms of trying to arrive at certain timesaving yet fair means. Mr. Fila voiced no opposition to the concept of videolink. Am I fair to represent that? If the Bench would permit me to make that representation. In terms of other issues such as the order of crossing those accused who have already given direct, there is as to -- there appears to be one counsel who does not necessarily go along with what appears to have been represented earlier in the record by the other counsel. And I think that may be an issue where we may not arrive at agreement, but we are trying to do that. We are trying very hard, and I want to say that I was very gratified that there was this much cooperation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We should perhaps now proceed counsel by counsel. Actually, Ms. Somers, you should perhaps now address the issue individually per accused and then the Defence counsel can respond. Perhaps you should now analyse positions of individual Defence teams and then later on we will hear their response, again individually, so that we can save some time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if it might facilitate things, just to go in the order of our response, if everyone has it, it could give a certain flow to it that might make it go faster. Starting on page 5 of our response, I would like to say that Mr. Krstan Simic has kindly rectified the problem of the names of the witnesses. Has everyone had a chance, I hope, to find it? So that is one issue that is okay. Witness AK continues to be a matter which we will have to seek resolution on. Let me just go through this. Otherwise everything else on page 5 is okay. No concerns there. Turning to -- on page 9, paragraph 23; page 9, paragraph 23, it concerns the accused Kvocka. The submission contains no information about two of the witnesses contained in its witness list in attachment III. The names -- I don't know whether or not I'm at liberty to raise these or to voice these. If this could be addressed, we would be very grateful. Nothing on page 10. And then on page 11, paragraph 27, the use -- or considering as an exhibit or including on the exhibit list psychiatric examinations is, in our judgement, inappropriate. These are in fact subject to Rule 94 bis and all those Rules must govern. So if those Rules are complied with with the relevant time period and our opportunity to challenge or not, then I think that would cure it, but they do not belong properly on this type of exhibit list. This has covered our concerns, and if the Chamber would like us to come back and address anything after Defence response, we would be happy to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, Krstan Simic, would you like to respond at this point so that we can proceed individually? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. At the meeting that we held with the Office of the Prosecutor, they indicated a certain number of problems and we accepted their objections, and we submitted a brief in which we explained these issues, elucidated them. We have submitted the list of witnesses. We plan to call 26 witnesses and we have indicated 4 alternative witnesses. We followed the intentions of the Chamber as regards the use of affidavits. A witness will testify on a particular fact and then we will have a witness testifying by way of affidavits on that fact. I don't think that we are required to disclose them at this point because they will be introduced five days prior to the appearance of the witness, because witnesses might fail to appear, and we believe that we will be in full compliance of Rule 94 ter. As regards the request of the Prosecutor to cross-examine witnesses who will testify via affidavit, we are not in a position to effect the decision of the Chamber. We do object to that decision, but it is within the discretion of the Chamber. The Chamber will decide whether there is a need for those witnesses to be cross-examined. We are somewhat concerned as regards this problem. We do not wish this to become a strategy of the Prosecutor, that is, to cross-examine each witness testifying via affidavits. In that way, I think we will bring into question the very existence of this institution, of this institute, this particular procedure, or rather a tool which we believe to be very useful here. We decided to call Witness AK in our case. This particular witness has been -- was called by the Prosecutor. The Prosecutor has expressed its opposition to our calling this particular witness, and to that effect it has cited the case law of this Chamber, stating that on one particular occasion this type of request was rejected. However, I must remind you of the practice of the Office of the Prosecutor. They prevented the Defence from communicating with Prosecution witnesses. On one particular occasion I requested such opportunity, such access to their witnesses, and that request of mine was rejected. Thereby it was not possible for us to elucidate certain very important facts. There is something specific as regards our request. The Chamber has spent a lot of time addressing the issue of exhibits, the admissibility of statements given by witnesses to the Office of the Prosecutor. As regards Witness AK, his statement was admitted because he was one of the first witnesses in the case, and it became a part of the record. However, in a later decision, the statement was withdrawn. That particular statement contains a number of crucial facts which we didn't discuss because they were contained in the statement that Witness AK gave to the Office of the Prosecutor. By this later decision, those facts were redacted from the file -- from the record, rather. They do not exist on the record. So that is the reason why we should like to ask the Chamber to enable us to call once again Witness AK, who is ready to come here and testify pursuant to our request, because that witness will certainly make his contribution in the truth-finding process. The second issue that was broached by the response of the Prosecutor is the issue of exhibits concerning the accused Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, can I just clarify one point before you move on to exhibits? I understand that the 28 witnesses that are listed are all going to be, in your view, live witnesses who actually come to the courtroom; is that right? Any affidavit witnesses will be -- MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Twenty-six. Twenty-six, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Twenty-six, right. But all 26 will be live, and any affidavit witnesses will be in addition to the 26? I just want to make sure I understand that. Is that right? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Twenty-six plus fourteen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is a specific case in many respects. Any questions which are not directly linked to Omarska itself are extremely important when dealing with the question of the relationship of the accused Kvocka because he's charged with persecution. That is why the Defence will have to demonstrate certain things showing what his positions were, what his choices were, and that is why we have offered a certain number of exhibits. The Prosecution has objected to DP-57 and DP-58 from our list. I have to say that those are documents which I received from the Prosecution, in fact, and these are medical documents about the wounding of members of the security from the Omarska police station: Miroslav Nisic, referring to an event dated the 30th of May. Furthermore, the Prosecution is also objecting to Exhibits DP-59, 89, 90, 91, 92, and 93, 94/1, 94/2, and 94/3. I have to explain what this is all about. These are judgements of military courts, documents of military courts, which reveal a drastic attitude towards persons who fled or avoided being drafted. The sentences were drastic, and we wish to illustrate a time, a situation, an atmosphere, for the Chamber to be able fully to judge what possibility of choice the accused had at their disposal. Also we heard testimony here that Muslim vehicles were requisitioned as an element of persecution. We have tendered charges again to persons of Serb ethnicity to show that this was a regular practice in relation to other members of other ethnic groups, and Kerim Mesanovic spoke about this. Therefore, these are exhibits which can be highly relevant, and I see no reason why we should not offer them to the Chamber and allow the Chamber to judge their relevance rather than objecting to them even being tendered. As to the objection to the introduction into the record of expert witness reports, we accept the objection as those exhibits will be dealt with when the question of expert testimony is addressed. And to save time, I can immediately tell the Chamber that our intention is to submit a motion in which we will offer these reports and have them admitted without calling the expert witnesses because we don't see that to be necessary. But we have listed him just in case there could be any changes in the position of the Prosecution. So I think that we have resolved all the disputed issues except those that are up to the Chamber to rule on, that is, Witness AK and the question of these exhibits. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Mr. Simic, that there is a question which Ms. Susan Somers raised, that is, paragraph 23 of her response.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I address you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I believe that has been cleared up. Mr. Simic has provided us with an updated list. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Thank you very much, Mr. Krstan Simic. So, Ms. Susan Somers, in relation to the accused Kos.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we proceed with accused Kos, may we have just a moment to respond to these points while they're fresh in our minds, so that the Chamber is aware of what issues remain as to these points, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, of course. That is a better idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. As to Witness AK, the position, it's a bit puzzling to the Prosecution in that the witness, of course, did appear and was fully examined with opportunity to have the case -- with a required case to be put to the witness when the witness was in court. The notion of reliance now on statements, which has at all times been opposed by the Defence, seems a bit inconsistent and not a basis, certainly, for bringing back a witness who was here and whose statement was with the Defence and could have been used and incorporated ably into cross-examination at the time. Again, Rule 90 specifically states that one does put to the witness the case. There appears to be no basis for dragging a witness back when that witness could have, at the time, been fully and completely examined. I do not think that is the purpose of -- I don't think that that actually comports with the notion of a fresh witness list. It seems to skirt, in our judgement, the obligation of the Defence to completely examine a witness at the time on all materials that are before counsel. The Trial Chamber, on another occasion, on the 3rd of May, gave an oral order on the Prosecution's motion for protective measures in which the Prosecution requested -- we mentioned AK -- I'm sorry. We asked if we could contact AK and see if the witness wished to speak to the Defence. The witness did not wish to speak to the Defence any further. So I think we have done that which we can do. But it eludes us as to why, when all of this could have and should have, for judicial economy, been dealt with, it was not. On the issue of 94 bis, expert statements and submission, the Rule actually does not give the Defence -- does not lay the decision of whether or not live testimony would be required. If a challenge is raised to the report, then the right lies with the Prosecution to have that expert brought for cross-examination. We have indicated to counsel that we would exercise such right where we deem appropriate upon receipt -- a timely receipt of the 94 bis statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: As to the items referenced in paragraph 26, page 10 of our response, the DP-numbered items, the language of the paragraph, just to bring it to the Chamber's attention, is not one of objection, it is one of questioning the relevance. It specifically states, and I quote: "At this time, the Prosecution has no objection to the majority of the exhibits contained in this list. However, the Prosecution questions the relevance of the following exhibits ..." and goes on to itemise them. If the Chamber is satisfied as to the relevance, then this is what we had asked for further clarification upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, you can now continue with respect to the accused Kos. Let me tell you that we intend to make a break at about 11.30. Thank you for correcting me, Judge Riad. I said 10.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The discussion about the accused Kos in our document begins on page 11. The issues which have been raised that we wanted to bring to the Chamber's attention, again, we discussed -- I think the only real critical ones were the issues of deposition where we thought it would be inappropriate. We have raised that in response to Judge Wald's inquiry as to our overall position. The issues of -- I'm sorry. I think that's it. I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You oppose all nine deposition witnesses, it says in your motion here; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It would be our preference, Your Honour. Yes, we would oppose them. We think these witnesses are out of character and will present evidence which would require cross-examination before the Bench, so the Bench has a chance to observe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And that's on the grounds that they are -- all I know is from here; that's on the grounds that they were all guards?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Very much so, with the perspective that I believe, in the quest for truth, this Chamber should be able to inquire into.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. O'Sullivan? No, sorry. Mr. Nikolic, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: There is one other aspect to the Prosecution's submission that we discussed with the Prosecution a couple of days ago, and that's in paragraph 28. We seek some guidance from the Chamber and perhaps the registrar on the way in which we should designate witnesses for whom we seek protective measures, which pseudonym we could use to perhaps distinguish Defence witnesses as between themselves and from Prosecution witnesses who have pseudonyms. We will, of course, be seeking protection by way of motion and we'll do that forthwith. But can we be told how Your Honours would like us to designate our witnesses? We chose D2/A on the assumption that "D2" was the second accused Kos, and "A" being the first of his witnesses. But if you can tell us how you'd like it done, then we will file that request for protection early next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. O'Sullivan and myself have divided up one of the questions in the Prosecution's submission and that is the question of depositions, which is the only point raised in relation to the accused Kos. The question of deposition testimony has a long history. We have been discussing it ever since 1999. The Defence of the accused Kos, when suggesting and proposing deposition testimony, had in mind Rule 71 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The first sentence of that Rule reads: "... when that is in the interests of justice." I think that I don't need to explain that the Defence would like most of all to have all its witnesses present in the courtroom. The reasons why this is not possible have been explained as exceptional circumstances, and we have elaborated on that in our submissions so far. The reasons why the witnesses don't wish to come to The Hague and to this courtroom would require, in my mind, psychological treatment and explanations. Let me refer briefly to the key arguments of the Prosecution that they offer in opposing depositions. As far as the Defence has been able to understand, the only reason is due to the absence of visual contact, which enhances the credibility of the witness. It is the submission of the Defence that the credibility of the witness is determined by the content of his testimony, all the more so as Rule 71 envisages the possibility of cross-examination and that the Prosecution is in no way prejudiced as it does have the ability to cross-examine. No mention was made today of this, but I don't know whether the present Prosecution team is concerned by security reasons which were referred to quite frequently earlier on when depositions were discussed. I have to say that the previous team, led by Ms. Brenda Hollis, was explicit in its position that the Prosecution does not rely on security reasons; that it is ready to carry out deposition testimony, as suggested by the Defence, in Banja Luka. Therefore --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nikolic, excuse me for interrupting you, but I would like to see, if possible, whether you would consider the idea that I introduced into the discussion, that is, to revise your list, to abandon depositions, so as to have a combination of presence in the courtroom and affidavit statements, that is, statements under oath; or are you insisting on depositions? That is, in your opinion, would it be possible to make such a revision so as to have live witnesses and affidavit witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you're asking too much of me at this stage. I cannot tell you that without consulting the witnesses again. We have proposed nine witnesses for depositions. Now that we have the 65 ter briefs of the other Defence teams, we saw that two witnesses have been proposed to be heard in court. Whether they will come or not, I don't know. But as regarding the remaining seven, I would have to contact them to see whether one, two, or three of them would be ready to come here to the court and whether the others could testify by affidavits. But I cannot tell you at this stage. So to summarise, because of all the reasons that the witnesses are insisting on, not the Defence. It is the Defence's duty to try and meet their requests as much as possible, but in the interests of justice so that the truth may be heard. Of course, it is up to the Court to judge their testimony. We prefer deposition testimony as the first priority, and the second possibility would be a videolink, if the Chamber should so decide; this is to say, what we consider to be crucial is that those witnesses proposed by the Defence should not be moved from Banja Luka. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Madam Susan Somers, your comment, and then we will have the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, first of all, I want to reassure this Chamber and my counsel opposite that security issues for us are not at all an issue any more than they would be for anyone else present there from this Tribunal. That is not a factor. We are willing to go to Banja Luka. Ms. Hollis has been very firm on that and I continue, and that is our position. The category or genre of witness about whom we are speaking, I can envision posing a great deal of, shall we say, spirited examination. With this type of witness, Your Honours, in the absence of the Chamber which referees and monitors, of course, the delivery or the leading of evidence, I believe that it would be very difficult, given some of the roads down which we would hope to go on cross-examination, to elicit answers. In a deposition posture - and I have the greatest respect for the legal officers who would be handling it and I do not have a concern there - it concerns the ability to proceed orderly. Objections are only voiced on the record. If a witness does not answer, as he or she would have to do before this Chamber or face the consequences therefrom, it will impede the inquiry and it will cause having to do it again. I do not believe, in good faith, that there is any saving of either time or money if that is the case. Based on the experience of other trials, there are some very difficult witnesses and this genre of witness, many of whom will have their own problems which prohibit them, in their view, from attending live in The Hague, will not be willing, I am confident, to answer certain questions. Therefore, the Chamber, I believe, is the core -- the presence and participation and observance of the Chamber with this type of witness is essential in order to make an effective cross-examination in order to deliver to this Chamber the best possible evidence that we can deliver. I believe that we can certainly, with counsel, try to pare down those witnesses about whom this would be an issue and present it to this Chamber for consideration. But I believe that that will ultimately happen. Let's see. Was there any other point? I think those were the only concerns. Our discussions with Mr. Nikolic -- with the Nikolics and with Mr. O'Sullivan were very fruitful. It was my understanding at the time that it was either videolink or deposition. I didn't sense at the time that there was a distinction or preference. Nevertheless, I do want to emphasise our willingness. And, of course, we will send a member of the trial team to Banja Luka. It would not be without live participation from any of the staff that we deem appropriate. So the Court has our assurance that the security issue is not a concern, absent some grave change in circumstances. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that before we proceed with the accused Radic, we should have a break. It is true that the question of money and time is not essential, but it is certainly a factor affecting the organisation in justice. One has to have the time and the money that is required, and it is in this perspective that we are trying to discuss matters so as to organise, in the best possible manner, the presentation of evidence. I think that now is the time for the break. I apologise for not saying before that we intend to work in the following way: to have a half-hour break now and then to proceed until 1.00; if necessary, to continue in the afternoon. We would begin at about 2.30 until about 5.30, if necessary. So this is just for you to be able to organise your time. So a half-hour break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Let us resume our hearing. In view of our schedule, we're now going to hear the response of the Prosecutor as regards the accused Radic. Ms. Somers, let us hear you. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the benefit of all, this is contained at the very bottom of page 12 of our response, if it will help, and the actual text begins on page 13. Paragraph 31 brings into question on our part the report of Dr. -- as a courtesy preview, the report of Dr. Nenad Kecmanovic. The initial readings of this report have led us to believe that we will undoubtedly file a motion to exclude on relevance grounds, as well as bias. If in fact the Chamber deems it appropriate to admit the report under Rule 94 bis, we will clearly seek to cross-examine on this. And so this is both a relevance and, if we get beyond that and it goes in, 94 bis issue. That would also cover point 32. And then on point 33, again these are properly the subject of 94 bis and all the provisions which apply thereto. Paragraph 34, Dr. Beatovic, the issue would -- excuse me one second. We think the relevance is very questionable and urge the Chamber not to consider it. But should the Chamber consider the report, we would, under 94 bis's provision for challenge, challenge it. Moving on to paragraph 37 on page 14, the discussion of affidavits. The language that we think is particularly salient here is that affidavits, of course, are not to substitute for live testimony, only to add to, under the provisions of both the Rule and the appellate decision interpreting it. In this instance, accused Radic's first ten would provide evidence which goes to absolutely critical, fundamental issues of the indictment. For example, the group discussed in paragraph 37 discusses -- it would produce evidence on the position of the accused, which is critical for this Court to assess and for the Chamber to conclude as it will on it, based on the evidence. Cross-examination, in our view, is absolutely necessary to give a full, truthful picture of what these witnesses would have to say and should not be left to the untested method of affidavit. 38, the evidence concerns the behaviour of the accused Radic as well as the treatment of detainees, absolutely fundamental issues of this indictment, for which cross-examination should lie. Paragraph 39 goes to evidence of what actually happened in the camp. There are -- these are camp guards who were there and will tell you what they saw, what occurred, and the actions of accused Radic. Again, these are issues which are absolutely to the core of the indictment and are not properly the subject of affidavit. The appellate decision, of course, leaves great discretion to the Chamber and leaves it to be decided on a case-by-case basis, and in our judgement, these cases would be cases where affidavit would be inappropriate. Moving on to paragraph 40 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Is it your position that anybody who attempts to give any kind of evidence about anything that went on in the camp is going to be core and essential and couldn't be done, even if you could show a direct nexus under 94 ter, such as the Court of Appeals did require in the Kordic case? That appears to be your position, that if they were there in the camp, that anything they have to say about the camp or the position of anybody or anything is essential, core and, under your theory, shouldn't be the subject of an affidavit. I just want to see if that's basically your position.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Much of our position, Your Honour. It is not just what went on and about whom; it is the accused in the camp that they are being called to discuss, and this I believe would differentiate it from a general background of the camp as a camp. We are talking here about the accused Radic. And yes, in our view, under these circumstances, in this type of case-by-case analysis, this would not be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I understand that about the behaviour of Radic. I mean, I understand your position in 38. It's a little less clear about the position of him and the organisation of guard duty. And then in 39, it just says "apparently served as guards," and these witnesses -- and doesn't say whether those witnesses in 39, what they would testify about.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If in fact any of the evidence which -- having not seen the affidavits, any of the evidence which may be suggested - I'm sorry - which may be put forth goes to these issues, then we certainly would take that position. I would be better served if I had them in front of me to be able to represent to the Chamber what it is specifically, because I have only a general summary. But I think it is fair to say: In these cases, one who works in a camp will be privy to much information that can only come from an insider, and it would be our obligation to explore that fully to bring to the Chamber's attention and make sure that nothing is left out of the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So your core position appears to be --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Sorry. Your core position appears to be that anybody who is going to testify about the camp, about conditions or anything in the camp, can only do it by live or videolink?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: That's going to make for one long, long trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It is our hope, Judge Wald, that if we have -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Those who worked there, Your Honour, those people who were actually part of the machinery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right. Right, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And drawing that distinction, not just anyone who happened to perhaps have delivered food to the camp, unless there's a particular incident that must be addressed. But it may indeed require at the front end having a bit more time. However, if it turns out in the course of trying it by some other method -- and I just want to make sure that when the Bench refers to "live," it also contemplates videolink as live testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I meant -- I understand your position on videolink.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think in these instances, if we had to risk having to stop or come back or ask the Court to impose some type of sanction for failure to comply, which is, again, I think very realistic, it might be more judicially economical to try to do it quickly, in a well-fashioned, crisp cross-examination, live, get it over with, if that were -- hopefully that will be the way it will happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: It's a nice ideal to aim for, but, I mean, you know, your ending up the Prosecution case has taken a long time to get to that point. If we take every witness the Defence proposes, we would have somewhere in vicinity of 150 witnesses. And we know from experience they don't get up and everything goes boom, boom, boom and get down and the next -- you know, it takes a long time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We do try to present a reasonable position, factoring every consideration that the Chamber must account for. But again, if the Chamber is asking is this our position, it is. And if we are ordered to pare it down or if we have to try to come to an accommodation with counsel opposite, then we will try to do that. But yes, that is our position at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers, I should like to ask you a question as a follow-up to the question asked by Madam Judge Wald. I think that it is good to have -- it would be good, even ideal, to have here all of the victims who were detained in Omarska, and as regards the Defence, it would probably be ideal for them to hear all of the employees of the camp here in the courtroom, but we cannot do that, and I don't think that we are going to finish this case before the end of the next year if we proceed in that way. One should bear in mind the fact that it is not only the Chamber who has other commitments but also the Tribunal. We have to be realistic. Okay. We are going to continue in the same spirit, but at the end I will try to give you the appropriate guidelines so that everybody can adopt a realistic position. You know that we had many problems with the testimony of Prosecution witnesses. We cannot afford to have the same problem once again. We have to provide the Defence with adequate opportunity to prepare themselves and to prepare their case in an appropriate manner. We were badly affected with a series of changes that took place in this trial, and now I should like to hear the parties as regards their positions and we will see if it is possible to make an agreement and to find a compromise. If there is no such agreement, the Chamber will issue adequate ruling, with the view of bringing this case to its close. Sorry for having interrupted you, Ms. Somers. I just wanted to share my concerns and my confusion, to a certain extent, in this regard because we would end up hearing a number of people who were employees at the camp and we cannot afford to call them all. I assume that there was a great deal of them working at the camp. I just wish to express this concern of mine to you, Ms. Somers. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I appreciate that and I think it will help us in trying to reach some type of accord. I do want to indicate that should affidavits for some of these persons be accepted, if the Chamber would consider, if we raise an objection, permitting us to cross-examine only, not to reiterate live, but perhaps only to cross-examine in the location that is appropriate and limit it just to the points not requiring the live, complete testimony but simply cross on the affidavit testimony, if that might be a possible consideration as one possibility. If the Chamber, after we have had a chance to confer with our colleagues opposite, finds that we can make an order -- at least present to them our greatest concerns and then present that to the Chamber, that there are some for whom it would really be a no-go on an affidavit, a not-possible affidavit or not reasonable, and some who are corroborating, perhaps things that were said by those key witnesses, if the Chamber would consider that, we would also be grateful, as an alternative, if nothing else meets the time considerations. Moving on to paragraph -- let me see, I believe it was 40. I think the issue in paragraph 40 is that all these -- these persons essentially corroborate the testimony of two persons only. It's a -- besides the cumulative nature which generally offends Chambers, they are going, again, to very, very key issues. I would have to put this in the same category as my previous comments for the Chamber to consider. Paragraph 41, no problem. Paragraph 42, we are not in possession at this time of a list of exhibits. It did not accompany or become incorporated into the 65 ter papers submitted by the accused Radic's counsel, and we'd just ask if we can please have that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Ms. Somers. I think that Mr. Fila, he is going to refer to a list of exhibits as well. Mr. Fila, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I will tell you a nice surprise. I do not have any exhibits at all. In accordance with 65 ter, exhibits and documentary evidence are listed, if they exist, in a pre-Defence brief, but I don't have such evidence. All the written material that I have was actually tendered by the Prosecution, and I cannot offer anything that I don't have. I'm not going to have any documentary evidence, so I think that issue has been settled. This was referred to and discussed with the Prosecution yesterday. As regards the remaining issues, I shall try to be as brief as possible and to explain a couple of points. Though the situation looks complex, I don't think it will turn out to be that complex in the end. As regards experts, Professor Kecmanovic, in particular, you have his CV. He was a highly-placed official, and his report was paid for by the Tribunal and he received appropriate fees for his report. So I think that the Tribunal deems his report to be adequate and necessary. It is kind of a counterpart to the report presented by Witness Greve, whom we did not cross-examine or object to. In addition to two reports, the witness will be able to provide the Chamber with his expertise. If it is necessary to cross-examine him, well, let him be cross-examined. I personally think that a cross-examination is not necessary. I think that we would only be wasting time discussing something which was already discussed with Witness Greve. So the position of the Defence is as follows: Whoever started the war is now irrelevant. The Statute provides for individual responsibility of the accused. It is not necessary to establish who attacked whom in this war. What we have to establish is whether there were any crimes that were committed. So the reports given by experts such as Dr. Kecmanovic or Dr. Greve is something useful for the Court to have in order to establish what really happened in the former Yugoslavia. I apologise. But let me repeat once again: If the Prosecution requests a cross-examination, I will not oppose their request. As regards experts Dr. Ana Najman and Dr. van den Bussche, it was the Court who decided to hear this gentleman, to hire this gentleman. I don't know him, but I presume that it was the Court who decided that his report was adequate and useful, because he was actually appointed by the Court. I think that we will only be wasting time by cross-examining Dr. Ana Najman and Dr. Bernard van den Bussche. However, if the Prosecution wishes to do so, let them have the cross-examination of the witnesses. As regards Dr. Stanko Beatovic, he was heard on the same facts in the Kunarac case, and I will submit the relevant transcript of his testimony and also his written report that is currently being translated. I do not intend to call him for direct examination. However, I believe that it is necessary for the Prosecutor to cross-examine this particular expert witness. Why? In case this Court should establish that there was a rape, I think it would be very useful to hear this witness because he is an expert on the area and he was always heard as such in the Kunarac case. There is, however, something additional which is specific for this particular case. There is a slight difference which is contained in his report, which is currently being translated and will be submitted to the Prosecutor as soon as possible. According to the Statute, you are bound to take into account the judicial practice in the former Yugoslavia, and he discussed the topic in the Kunarac case. It would not be amiss to hear him once again or to read his written report. Either possibility is acceptable for this Defence team. I just wish to say once again that I was abiding by what you suggested, Your Honour, that is, that written reports be submitted and that no additional time is wasted for this matter. It is up to the Chamber to ascertain the quality and the usefulness of this report. As regards point 5, we submitted a list of 26 witnesses. Some of them will be called. We are not going to call anyone whose name is not on the list. We are perfectly aware of the fact that we cannot call 26 witnesses within ten days. But we will definitely call some of them and hear them in the period of two weeks. Should the videolink be opted for as a solution in respect of those witnesses, then we would bring only three of those 26 witnesses and the remaining 23 would be heard via videolink, if this is less costly for the Tribunal. So this number of 26 witnesses is only a tentative figure because we cannot hear as many witnesses in two weeks' time. As regards the issue of affidavits, our position is as follows in this matter: A witness testifies and an affidavit accompanies him. If the Prosecution wants to cross-examine, in that case, the Court judges whether that is necessary or not. We believe it is not. But if the Trial Chamber judges that it is necessary, then this is done by videolink. That was the agreement that we reached with the Prosecution. A matter of principle which I should like to raise: You can organise that only once you have reviewed the affidavits which we will submit. That is something that I will do on behalf of Radic; that I will provide the Chamber and the Prosecution with all the statements and all the affidavits more than a month prior to my turn so that you will be fully aware of what is going to be said. So if the Chamber allows cross-examination, there will be adequate time for that to be organised. I wish to underline that the people for whom affidavits are taken do not wish to come to The Hague, but they are ready to be cross-examined either by deposition or by videolink in Banja Luka or by taking an official statement under oath before a legal officer. So that would be the procedure. A witness, affidavits, and cross-examination only by videolink in Banja Luka. This applies to all the affidavits that we intend to submit. Let me add one further point. It is not up to the Prosecution to judge the value of affidavits and what they contain. Those are people who are here or there and it is up to them to testify. I can't bring people from Rwanda to say that Mladjo Radic was the shift leader or not. This can only be said by someone who was there. I have no other witnesses. They were either victims or they were guards. These guards are afraid to come. We will hear them by videolink in all cases when the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber considers it necessary. But I don't think you should be unnecessarily concerned, that is, regarding all the affidavits that the Prosecution seems to be uncomfortable about. As for paragraph 41, the affidavit of Idriz Mujkic, to save on costs and out of my respect for Mr. Niemann, I asked him to be kind enough to take an affidavit from this person and he did so, Mr. Niemann himself, in person. I told my learned friend, Ms. Somers, "If that man testifies on the trivial fact that Mladjo Radic assisted him, gave him a transistor radio or something - it doesn't matter - if the Prosecution is of the opinion that cross-examination is necessary, they can bring him here to The Hague." But this entails a great deal of cost and I don't know how I would be able to do that. If the Prosecution can do it, then let them do it at the expense of the time given to me -- I mean within my time. And, finally, the last point I wish to make has to do with Witness K. By omission of the Prosecution, I was not able to see a statement of her's and she will be brought here by courtesy of Mr. Saxon. It will be at the expense of their time but at my request to answer questions that she was not able to answer because I wasn't given the document in time. So, as you see, it won't take too long. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Fila. Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to avoid having the wrath of the second floor on my shoulders, it is the Victims and Witnesses Unit which will handle bringing that witness and not Mr. Saxon. We will certainly facilitate in any way we can to make sure that this happens. On paragraph 41, about the individual to whom reference is made, I just wanted to emphasise that we are simply reserving our right to call. We have not seen the affidavit. We will try to be reasonable. And if this was a matter that was agreed upon between Mr. Niemann and counsel, I'd just like to have a look at the affidavit that will be submitted. I'm sorry, the statement. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. We have given it to you. You have that statement. Ms. Brenda Hollis has it and Mr. Niemann gave it to me. So you had it before I had it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I have not had a chance to make the assessment, and I will get back to you on it. I apologise for that but time was not on my side. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So now we have come to the accused Mr. Zigic, Madam Susan Somers, so you have the floor again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, a number of issues had come up in the course of our discussions with counsel for Mr. Zigic. The first issue is referred to in paragraph 45, which can be found on page 18 of our document. The concern raised by us was transmitted to Mr. Stojanovic, and we simply called to his attention the provisions of Rule 75(D) which we believe apply here, and we simply passed on that considered judgement to him. On page 20, the particular incident is discussed where it says, line 1, "There are a number of names which I will not read out loud and we will have to correct the record. We apologise. There will be a corrigendum followed with pseudonyms. This was inadvertent." But the incident is a very notorious incident and there were days of testimony before the Chamber. Again, this would fall very much in a category of "need to go into evidence greatly." Paragraph 50 is a 94 bis matter and we'd simply indicate that those provisions would have to be invoked. Let me just take a quick look. The transcript testimony was of concern to us inasmuch as - this is my understanding after having read the record - the Prosecution was not able to introduce transcript testimony. We would ask the Chamber to consider whether or not that should be changed, essentially an equality of arms type posture, that transcript testimony had not been used before. A concern was raised about matters which are really not within the Prosecutor's bailiwick, of a concerned method of investigation by a Defence counsel. When raised to us, essentially as a courtesy, we simply suggested that counsel raise the issue, perhaps, in motion form to the Chamber, and I have seen this morning a motion that addresses the particular concern. So I believe that Mr. Stojanovic will raise that matter to the Chamber. Just so the Chamber knows, it was raised to us in this discussion which we held with Defence counsel. I believe at this point that's pretty much where we stand on that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Madam Susan Somers. Mr. Stojanovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I think that there are no major differences between us and the position of the Prosecution. There was a question raised regarding observance of the rules of confidentiality and the protection of certain witnesses who appeared earlier on in this Court. We are referring to Witness R from the Tadic case. However, from our submission, it is not possible to decipher the name of that witness. However, from the response of the Prosecution in paragraph 44, it is clear who this was. I have to raise the problem regarding this witness. Mr. Zigic has been charged with a very grave offence. We have heard here two or three, in our opinion, highly contradictory witnesses. One witness in the Tadic case, that is, this Witness R, in great detail and precision described that particular event. That witness was called as a witness for the Prosecution in our case too. However, in spite of all their efforts, the Prosecution did not manage to bring him in. The Defence would like that witness to be brought here. We fully agree with the Prosecution's suggestion that the witness be provided with full protective measures. However, in view of the fact that this witness is also a victim, did not respond to the invitation of the Prosecution, we're highly pessimistic that he will respond to an invitation from the Defence to appear. So we expect that we will have to appeal to the Trial Chamber for assistance in this case so that we might ensure his presence in this trial. In that context, the transcript from the Tadic case will show us to what extent that witness is relevant for this case and also highlight the necessity for such steps to be taken. Therefore, our submission of this exhibit can also be viewed in this light. The position of this Defence team is that your suggestion regarding affidavits is quite acceptable for us. If I may go back to this topic very briefly, the one that my learned friend Ms. Somers raised, this Defence team considers confidentiality of certain facts from the indictment to be a very serious obstacle and we have made a written submission dated the 5th of January. We are not quite sure whether it has reached you, Your Honours, whether you have received it. The gist of it is that confidential attachments to the indictment prevent us from interviewing people about what the indictment charges our client with. We have to ask whether Mr. Zigic participated in the killing of a certain person or the beating up of a certain person. However, with these confidential schedules, we have no right to mention the name of the victim. I have made this submission. Unfortunately, it doesn't appear to have reached you. Maybe I have taken advantage of the time for this digression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Stojanovic. I do wish to interrupt and tell you that we have received this motion from you, so that you should know. We have been informed about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I consider this to be a problem for us in preparing our Defence case, and I think that the confidentiality should be rescinded, and, as a matter of principle, we are against the victims being held secret. However, by our objection, we do not intend in any way to call in question the established timetable for the continued proceedings, and please accept this as an expression of our wish to fully cooperate with the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Because, in my judgement, anything concerning the particular witness would require a moment of private session, is it possible to have a moment of private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, perhaps it would be appropriate. We have planned a private session at the end, but never mind. Just to deal with this point very briefly, we'll go into private session now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
